stem: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(A + B + C = \pi\). Show that \(\cos^{2} A + \cos^{2} B - \cos^{2} C = 1 - 2\sin A\sin B\cos C\).
The value of \(\sin (n+1)A\,\sin (n+2)A + \cos (n+1)A\,\cos (n+2)A\) is equal to
_derivation: This is cos X cos Y + sin X sin Y = cos(X - Y) with X = (n+2)A and Y = (n+1)A. The difference is (n+2)A - (n+1)A = A, so the expression equals cos A. Independent of n, which is the point of the question. Options are pairwise distinct (no twin).

stem: If \(\tan A - \tan B = x\) and \(\cot B - \cot A = y\) then \(\cot (A - B) = \) \(\ldots\)
_derivation: cot B - cot A = 1/tan B - 1/tan A = (tan A - tan B)/(tan A tan B) = x/(tan A tan B) = y, so tan A tan B = x/y. Then cot(A - B) = (1 + tan A tan B)/(tan A - tan B) = (1 + x/y)/x = (y + x)/(xy) = 1/x + 1/y. Verified numerically with A = 50 deg, B = 20 deg: x = 1.19175 - 0.36397 = 0.82778, y = 2.74748 - 0.83910 = 1.90838; 1/x + 1/y = 1.20805 + 0.52400 = 1.73205 and cot(30 deg) = 1.73205. Options A and B are negatives of each other, C and D are distinct - no twin.

stem: If \(\sin\theta = n\sin (\theta + 2\alpha)\) then \(\tan (\theta + \alpha)\) is equal to
_derivation: Put phi = theta + alpha, so theta = phi - alpha and theta + 2alpha = phi + alpha. The condition becomes sin(phi - alpha) = n sin(phi + alpha), i.e. sin phi cos alpha - cos phi sin alpha = n(sin phi cos alpha + cos phi sin alpha). Collecting: sin phi cos alpha (1 - n) = cos phi sin alpha (1 + n), so tan phi = [(1+n)/(1-n)] tan alpha. Note B is the reciprocal-shaped decoy (1-n)/(1+n); the two are not equal, so no twin.

stem: The value of \(\dfrac{\cos\theta}{1 + \sin\theta}\) is equal to\(\ldots\ldots\)
_derivation: With t = theta/2: cos theta = cos^2 t - sin^2 t = (cos t - sin t)(cos t + sin t) and 1 + sin theta = (cos t + sin t)^2. Hence the ratio = (cos t - sin t)/(cos t + sin t) = (1 - tan t)/(1 + tan t) = tan(pi/4 - t) = tan(pi/4 - theta/2). Checked at theta = 0: LHS = 1 and tan(pi/4) = 1. Checked at theta = 60 deg: LHS = 0.5/1.86603 = 0.26795 and tan(45 - 30) = tan 15 deg = 0.26795. Twin check: A = -C and B = -D, so although the four options pair up by sign no two are EQUAL.

stem: The value of \(\cos A\,\cos (60^\circ - A)\,\cos (60^\circ + A)\) is equal to\(\ldots\ldots\)
_derivation: cos(60 - A)cos(60 + A) = cos^2 60 - sin^2 A = 1/4 - sin^2 A. Multiplying by cos A gives cos A/4 - sin^2 A cos A = cos A/4 - (1 - cos^2 A)cos A = cos^3 A - (3/4)cos A = (1/4)(4cos^3 A - 3cos A) = (1/4)cos 3A. Checked at A = 0: LHS = 1 x 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.25 and (1/4)cos 0 = 0.25. All four options are distinct multiples.

By sin(pi - x) = sin x the last three factors repeat the first three: sin(13pi/14) = sin(pi/14), sin(11pi/14) = sin(3pi/14), sin(9pi/14) = sin(5pi/14), while sin(7pi/14) = sin(pi/2) = 1. So the product = [sin(pi/14) sin(3pi/14) sin(5pi/14)]^2. Converting to cosines (sin(pi/14) = cos(3pi/7), sin(3pi/14) = cos(2pi/7), sin(5pi/14) = cos(pi/7)) gives the standard cos(pi/7)cos(2pi/7)cos(3pi/7) = 1/8, so the answer is (1/8)^2 = 1/64. Numerically: 0.2225209 x 0.6234898 x 0.9009689 = 0.1250000, squared = 0.015625 = 1/64. All four options are distinct.

subtopic: Trigonometric Functions of Angles of a Triangle
stem: If \(\alpha + \beta + \varkappa = \pi\) then the value of \(\sin^{2}\alpha + \sin^{2}\beta - \sin^{2}\varkappa\) is equal to\(\ldots\ldots\)
_note: PRINTED NOTATION: the book denotes the third angle by the curly-kappa glyph ϰ (varkappa), not the conventional γ, in both the stem and options B–D. Verified at 5x zoom on p-22 (printed p.57) - it is unambiguously ϰ, not γ or a broken γ. Transcribed as \varkappa to stay faithful.
_derivation: This is the triangle identity sin^2 A + sin^2 B - sin^2 C = 2 sin A sin B cos C, which the book itself proves as solved example iii) on printed p.53 (page image p-18). Checked at alpha = beta = kappa = 60 deg: LHS = 0.75 + 0.75 - 0.75 = 0.75 and 2(0.86603)(0.86603)(0.5) = 0.75. Option B (with cos on the middle factor) gives 2(0.86603)(0.5)(0.86603) = 0.375, and D gives 1.29904 - both fail; A is not even symmetric. No twin.
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the third angle of the triangle is set with the curly-kappa glyph \(\varkappa\) rather than \(\gamma\), in the stem and in three of the four alternatives. Transcribed as printed.]

Since \(\alpha + \beta + \varkappa = \pi\), we have \(\alpha + \varkappa = \pi - \beta\), so \(\sin(\alpha+\varkappa) = \sin\beta\).

Applying the standard identity \(\sin^{2}A - \sin^{2}B = \sin(A+B)\sin(A-B)\),

\(\sin^{2}\alpha - \sin^{2}\varkappa = \sin(\alpha+\varkappa)\,\sin(\alpha-\varkappa) = \sin\beta\,\sin(\alpha-\varkappa)\).

Therefore \(\sin^{2}\alpha + \sin^{2}\beta - \sin^{2}\varkappa = \sin^{2}\beta + \sin\beta\,\sin(\alpha-\varkappa) = \sin\beta\left(\sin\beta + \sin(\alpha-\varkappa)\right)\).

Replacing the inner \(\sin\beta\) by \(\sin(\alpha+\varkappa)\) gives \(\sin(\alpha+\varkappa) + \sin(\alpha-\varkappa) = 2\sin\alpha\,\cos\varkappa\), so the value is \(2\sin\alpha\,\sin\beta\,\cos\varkappa\).

Hence (C).

stem: Let \(0 < A,\ B < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) satisfying the equation \(3\sin^{2} A + 2\sin^{2} B = 1\) and \(3\sin 2A - 2\sin 2B = 0\) then \(A + 2B\) is equal to\(\ldots.\)
_derivation: From the first equation 3sin^2 A = 1 - 2sin^2 B = cos 2B. From the second, sin 2B = (3/2)sin 2A = 3 sin A cos A. Then cos(A + 2B) = cos A cos 2B - sin A sin 2B = cos A (3 sin^2 A) - sin A (3 sin A cos A) = 0. Since 0 < A < pi/2 and 0 < 2B < pi we have 0 < A + 2B < 3pi/2, and the only zero of cosine strictly inside that range is pi/2 (3pi/2 is excluded by the strict inequalities). Hence A + 2B = pi/2. All four options are distinct.

subtopic: Trigonometric Functions of Angles of a Triangle
stem: In \(\Delta ABC\) if \(\cot A\,\cot B\,\cot C > 0\) then the triangle is\(\ldots.\)
_derivation: A triangle has at most one non-acute angle. If all three angles are acute every cotangent is positive and the product is positive. If one angle is right its cotangent is 0 and the product is 0, not > 0. If one angle is obtuse its cotangent is negative while the other two are positive, so the product is negative. Hence the product is positive exactly when the triangle is acute angled. D is a special case of B and therefore also gives product 0.

stem: The numerical value of \(\tan 20^\circ\,\tan 80^\circ\,\cot 50^\circ\) is equal to\(\ldots\ldots\)
_note: PRINTED TYPOGRAPHY: this stem sets the degree marks as superscript zeros (tan20⁰ tan80⁰ cot50⁰) whereas Misc II Q1 on the facing column sets the same expression with proper degree signs. Transcribed with ^\circ throughout; no mathematical ambiguity.
_derivation: cot 50 deg = tan 40 deg, so the product is tan 20 tan 40 tan 80 = tan 20 tan(60 - 20) tan(60 + 20), which by the identity tan theta tan(60 - theta) tan(60 + theta) = tan 3theta equals tan 60 deg = sqrt(3). Numerically 0.3639702 x 5.6712818 x 0.8390996 = 1.7320508 = sqrt(3). Cross-confirmed by the book itself: Misc II Q1 on the same spread asks the student to PROVE this product equals sqrt(3). All four options are distinct.

subtopic: Trigonometric Functions of Angles of a Triangle
stem: In any triangle \(ABC\), \(\sin A - \cos B = \cos C\) then prove that \(\angle B = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
_note: PRINTED WORDING: the book writes “In any triangle ABC, sin A − cosB = cosC then ∠B = π/2”, omitting the conditional “if”; only “prove that” has been carried in from the part-(II) instruction “Prove the following.” The word order is otherwise the book’s.
solution: [Textbook misprint: the conclusion is incomplete. From \(\sin A = \cos B + \cos C\) the cancellation gives \(\cos\dfrac{A}{2} = \cos\dfrac{B-C}{2}\), hence \(A = |B - C|\), which admits TWO branches — \(A = B - C\) giving \(\angle B = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) (the printed answer) and \(A = C - B\) giving \(\angle C = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\). The triangle \(A = 30^\circ, B = 60^\circ, C = 90^\circ\) satisfies the hypothesis with \(\angle B\) NOT a right angle. A scan over all triangles found no solutions outside these two families. The printed branch is proved above. The stem also omits the conditional 'if'.]

stem: Prove that \(\dfrac{\tan^{3} x}{1 + \tan^{2} x} + \dfrac{\cot^{3} x}{1 + \cot^{2} x} = \sec x\,\operatorname{cosec} x - 2\sin x\,\cos x\).

_note: PRINTED NOTATION: the book marks the angle as radian measure by a superscript c on π in the numerator (πᶜ/8), transcribed verbatim as \dfrac{\pi^{c}}{8}. The very next question (Misc II Q27) writes the same kind of angle as plain π/8 with no c — an internal inconsistency in the book, not a mathematical difference.
